questions.q: If a user is a member of db_datareader (which GRANTs SELECT on every table) but also has an explicit DENY SELECT on one specific table, what happens?
options: Both take effect, allowing partial access to the table
SQL Server throws an error because the two statements conflict
The DENY wins — SELECT on that table is blocked, regardless of the role membership
The GRANT from the role wins, since role grants always take precedence
questions.explain: DENY is an explicit block that overrides every GRANT, from any source, including through role membership.

options: Deletes the security principal entirely
Removes an explicit GRANT or DENY statement, without implying the opposite or affecting permissions from other sources like role membership
Always results in a DENY being applied automatically
Grants the exact opposite permission of whatever was previously set
questions.explain: REVOKE erases one explicit statement — it doesn't flip GRANT into DENY or vice versa, and it leaves permissions from other paths (like roles) untouched.

questions.q: Why is DENY useful for a scenario like "everyone in this broad role except this one sensitive table"?
options: DENY only works when there is no role membership at all
A single DENY statement overrides the role's broad GRANT without requiring any change to the role membership itself
DENY automatically removes the user from the role
DENY and GRANT cannot both apply to the same table
questions.explain: DENY lets you carve out an exception from a broad role grant with one targeted statement, leaving the role and its membership completely unchanged.

questions.q: Does this course's foundation, T-SQL Development, already cover GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE?
options: Yes, but only the REVOKE statement
Yes, in its final chapter on warehousing
Yes, in the same lesson that covered window functions
No — T-SQL Development's 118 lessons stayed entirely on the query-writing side of SQL and never covered this syntax
questions.explain: This is genuinely new syntax for this course to introduce — it isn't a recap of anything covered in the prerequisite T-SQL course.

questions.q: After REVOKE SELECT ON Sales.Orders FROM reporting_app runs (removing a previous explicit GRANT), if reporting_app is separately a member of db_datareader, what is the resulting access?
options: reporting_app still has SELECT access through the db_datareader role — REVOKE only removed the explicit GRANT, not the role-based access
An explicit DENY is automatically applied
reporting_app loses all access to every table in the database
reporting_app is automatically removed from db_datareader
questions.explain: REVOKE only undoes the one explicit statement it targets; any access coming from a different source, like role membership, remains completely intact.
